THORAX__Applied / Clinical Anatomy:
Why this matters: the thorax is where anatomy becomes procedural — you put needles and drains between ribs, you auscultate valves at surface landmarks, and you read referred pain from the diaphragm and pericardium. Master the intercostal neurovascular bundle, the pleural recesses, the diaphragm’s openings and the cardiac surface markings, and the emergencies (tension pneumothorax, tamponade, aortic dissection) become anatomy you can act on.
The Intercostal Space — Drains, Aspiration & Blocks
The neurovascular bundle
  • Runs in the costal groove at the inferior border of the rib above, ordered top → bottom Vein, Artery, Nerve (“VAN”)
  • Posteriorly the arteries come from the thoracic aorta; anteriorly from the internal thoracic artery
  • A smaller collateral bundle runs along the superior border of the rib below
Golden rule for needles & drains
  • Insert just above the upper border of the lower rib — away from the main bundle in the groove above
  • Chest drain → the “triangle of safety”: anterior border of latissimus dorsi, lateral border of pectoralis major, a line above the 5th intercostal space (nipple level), apex at the axilla
  • Intercostal nerve block targets the nerve in the costal groove
Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis (do not wait for an X-ray): respiratory distress, absent breath sounds, hyper-resonance, tracheal deviation away from the side, distended neck veins, hypotension. Treat with immediate needle/finger decompression (5th intercostal space, anterior/mid-axillary line — the safe triangle) then a chest drain.
Rib Fractures & Flail Chest
Middle ribs (5–9) are the most commonly fractured.
1st/2nd rib # = high-energy trauma — look for great-vessel & brachial-plexus injury.
Lower ribs (9–12) # → risk of spleen (left), liver (right) or kidney injury.
Flail chest = ≥2 ribs each broken in ≥2 places → a segment moves paradoxically (in on inspiration); underlying lung contusion drives the hypoxia.
Pleura, Recesses & Pneumothorax
The two layers
  • Visceral pleura — on the lung; autonomic supply → insensitive to pain
  • Parietal pleura — on the wall; costal/cervical parts by the intercostal nerves (T1–T11), central diaphragmatic + mediastinal by the phrenic (C3–C5) → pain (localised at the wall, referred to the shoulder centrally)
  • Costodiaphragmatic (costophrenic) recess — the lowest pleural space, where fluid collects; the lung does not fill it in quiet breathing
Air & fluid in the space
  • Pneumothorax — air in the pleural space → lung collapse; tension if a one-way valve pushes the mediastinum across
  • Pleural effusion — fluid; blunts the costophrenic angle; aspirate posteriorly, above the rib
  • Haemothorax (blood), empyema (pus), chylothorax (thoracic-duct lymph)
Lungs — Surface Markings, Auscultation & Aspiration
Surface markings
  • Apex ~2–3 cm above the medial third of the clavicle (vulnerable in neck procedures)
  • Lung inferior border crosses rib 6 (midclavicular), 8 (midaxillary), 10 (paravertebral); the pleura runs two ribs lower — 8, 10, 12
  • Oblique fissure ≈ 6th rib (both lungs); horizontal fissure (right only) ≈ 4th rib
Aspiration of a foreign body
  • The right main bronchus is wider, shorter & more vertical → inhaled objects lodge here
  • Right lung has 3 lobes, left has 2 (+ lingula) — the left makes room for the heart (cardiac notch)
The Diaphragm — Openings, Phrenic Nerve & Referred Pain
LevelOpeningStructures
T8Caval opening (in the central tendon)IVC + right phrenic nerve
T10Oesophageal hiatus (in the muscle)Oesophagus + anterior & posterior vagal trunks
T12Aortic hiatus (behind the diaphragm)Aorta + thoracic duct + azygos vein
“I 8 (ate) 10 EGgs AT 12”. IVC = T8; Esophagus + vaGus = T10; Aorta + Thoracic duct = T12. The phrenic nerve (C3–C5) gives all the motor supply and sensation to the central diaphragm (the peripheral rim is sensory via the lower intercostal/subcostal nerves) — “C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive.” Because of this, irritation of the central diaphragm (subphrenic abscess, blood, gallbladder) refers pain to the shoulder tip (C4 dermatome).
The Heart — Surface Anatomy, Valves & Coronaries
Auscultation areas (“APT-M”)
  • Aortic — 2nd intercostal space, right sternal edge
  • Pulmonary — 2nd intercostal space, left sternal edge
  • Tricuspid — 4th/5th ICS, left sternal edge
  • Mitral — 5th ICS, midclavicular line (the apex beat)
Coronary territories → MI
  • LAD → anterior wall & septum (V1–V4)
  • Circumflex → lateral wall (I, aVL, V5–V6)
  • RCA → inferior wall (II, III, aVF); supplies the SA node (~60%) & AV node (~90%) → inferior MI can cause bradyarrhythmia/heart block
Cardiac tamponade. Fluid in the pericardial sac — constrained by the non-compliant fibrous pericardium — compresses the heart → Beck’s triad (hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds) + pulsus paradoxus. Relieve by pericardiocentesis (subxiphoid, aiming to the left shoulder). The pericardium’s pain is carried by the phrenic nerve → referred to the shoulder/neck.
Mediastinum, Great Vessels & the Oesophagus
Mediastinum & SVC
  • The sternal angle (of Louis, T4/5) marks: the 2nd costal cartilage, the tracheal bifurcation, the start/end of the aortic arch, and the superior/inferior mediastinal boundary
  • SVC obstruction (usually lung cancer) → facial/arm swelling, distended neck veins, Pemberton’s sign
Aorta & recurrent laryngeal nerve
  • Arch branches: brachiocephalic, left common carotid, left subclavian
  • The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the arch at the ligamentum arteriosum → hoarseness with an aortic aneurysm or apical lung tumour (Ortner’s syndrome)
  • Coarctation → radio-femoral delay, upper-limb hypertension, rib notching; traumatic aortic rupture classically at the tethered isthmus
Oesophageal constrictions (sites of dysphagia, stricture & impacted foreign bodies): the cricopharyngeus (~15 cm), the aortic arch + left main bronchus (~25 cm), and the diaphragmatic hiatus (~40 cm). A left atrial enlargement can also indent it.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Neurovascular bundle = VAN in the costal groove of the rib above → insert needles/drains just above the lower rib.
Triangle of safety for a chest drain: lat dorsi, pec major, 5th intercostal space.
Tension pneumothorax = clinical diagnosis; decompress before imaging; trachea deviates away.
Parietal pleura hurts (intercostal + phrenic); visceral pleura does not (autonomic).
Costophrenic recess collects effusions; aspirate posteriorly above the rib.
Diaphragm: T8 IVC, T10 oesophagus + vagi, T12 aorta + thoracic duct; phrenic C3–5 → shoulder-tip referred pain.
Right main bronchus is more vertical → inhaled objects go right.
RCA supplies the SA & AV nodes → inferior MI → bradycardia/heart block. Tamponade = Beck’s triad.
THORAX__Thoracic Wall & Osteology:
Why this matters: the thoracic cage is a mobile bony box — rigid enough to protect the heart & lungs, springy enough to change shape with every breath. Learn the bones, their joints and the intercostal muscle layers, and both the surface landmarks you count from and the mechanics of ventilation fall out of the scaffold.
The Bony Cage — Overview
Components
  • Sternum anteriorly; 12 pairs of ribs + their costal cartilages laterally; 12 thoracic vertebrae posteriorly
  • The thoracic inlet (superior aperture) = T1 body, the 1st ribs & the manubrium — structures pass to/from the neck & upper limb here
  • The thoracic outlet (inferior aperture) is closed by the diaphragm
Functions
  • Protects the heart, lungs & great vessels
  • Provides the bellows for ventilation (changes thoracic volume)
  • Anchors muscles of the upper limb, back, neck & abdomen
The Sternum
Three parts
  • Manubrium — with the jugular (suprasternal) notch and clavicular notches; articulates with the clavicle & 1st costal cartilage
  • Body — receives the 2nd–7th costal cartilages
  • Xiphoid process — cartilaginous in youth, ossifies with age
Sternal angle (of Louis)
  • The manubriosternal joint — a palpable transverse ridge
  • Marks the 2nd costal cartilage → the reference point for counting ribs
  • Lies at the T4/5 disc: the tracheal bifurcation, the aortic arch, and the superior/inferior mediastinal boundary
The Ribs

Twelve pairs, classed by their anterior attachment:

TypeRibsAnterior attachment
True (vertebrosternal)1–7Directly to the sternum via their own costal cartilage
False (vertebrochondral)8–10To the cartilage of the rib above (forming the costal margin)
Floating (free)11–12No anterior attachment
A typical rib (3–9)
  • Head — two facets, articulating with its own vertebra & the one above
  • Neck → tubercle (articular facet for the transverse process)
  • Angle, then the shaft with the costal groove (inferior border — holds the neurovascular bundle)
Atypical ribs (1, 2, 10–12)
  • 1st rib — broadest, shortest, most curved; a single head facet; the scalene tubercle separates the grooves for the subclavian vein (front) and artery + T1 (behind)
  • 2nd rib — tuberosity for serratus anterior
  • 10th–12th — single head facet; 11 & 12 have no neck or tubercle
Thoracic Vertebrae & the Costal Joints
Thoracic vertebra features
  • Costal demifacets on the body (superior & inferior) for the rib heads
  • Transverse costal facets for the rib tubercles
  • Long, downward-sloping spinous processes; heart-shaped body
Two costovertebral articulations
  • Joint of the head — rib head with the demifacets of two adjacent vertebrae
  • Costotransverse joint — rib tubercle with the transverse process
  • Both are synovial & allow the rib to rotate/glide during breathing
Sternocostal joints. The 1st costal cartilage joins the manubrium by a primary cartilaginous (synchondrosis) joint (no movement); the 2nd–7th are synovial plane joints. The manubriosternal joint is a secondary cartilaginous (symphysis); the xiphisternal joint is a cartilaginous joint that usually ossifies with age.
Intercostal Muscles & the Neurovascular Plane
Three layers
  • External intercostals — fibres run infero-anteriorly (“hands in pockets”); elevate the ribs (inspiration); deficient anteriorly (external intercostal membrane)
  • Internal intercostals — fibres run infero-posteriorly; depress the ribs (forced expiration); deficient posteriorly
  • Innermost intercostals — the deepest layer
The neurovascular plane
  • Lies between the internal & innermost intercostals, in the costal groove
  • Order top → bottom: Vein, Artery, Nerve (“VAN”)
  • Intercostal nerves = the anterior rami of T1–T11; T12 is the subcostal nerve
Blood Supply — the Internal Thoracic Artery
Arteries
  • Internal thoracic (mammary) artery — from the subclavian; descends ~1 cm lateral to the sternum behind the costal cartilages
  • Gives the anterior intercostal arteries (upper spaces) & ends by dividing into the superior epigastric & musculophrenic arteries
  • Posterior intercostal arteries come from the thoracic aorta (upper two from the costocervical trunk)
Veins & clinical
  • Anterior intercostal veins → internal thoracic veins; posterior intercostal veins → the azygos system
  • The left internal thoracic artery (LIMA) is the gold-standard coronary bypass graft
Mechanics of Breathing
Diaphragm descent — increases the vertical diameter (the main driver of quiet inspiration).
Pump-handle (upper ribs + sternum move up & forward) — increases the antero-posterior diameter.
Bucket-handle (lower ribs swing up & out) — increases the transverse diameter.
Quiet expiration is passive — elastic recoil of the lungs & chest wall.
Muscles of respiration. Quiet inspiration: diaphragm + external intercostals. Forced inspiration adds accessories: scalenes, sternocleidomastoid, pectoralis major/minor, serratus anterior. Forced expiration: abdominal wall muscles + internal intercostals (quiet expiration is passive).
Surface Anatomy & Clinical Notes
Landmarks
  • Sternal angle = rib 2 = the count-from point; jugular notch ≈ T2
  • Costal margin = the 7th–10th cartilages; the subcostal angle at the xiphisternum
  • Nipple ≈ 4th intercostal space (in the male); the xiphisternal joint ≈ T9
Clinical
  • Cervical rib (extra rib off C7) → thoracic outlet syndrome (compresses the lower plexus / subclavian artery)
  • Pectus excavatum (sunken) / carinatum (pigeon chest) — sternal deformities
  • Rib notching on X-ray = collateral flow (e.g. aortic coarctation)
🧠 Mnemonics
Rib types — True 1–7, False 8–10, Floating 11–12.
External intercostals — fibres run like “hands in your pockets” (down & forward); they aid inspiration.
Neurovascular order — VAN (Vein, Artery, Nerve) top→bottom in the costal groove.
Sternal angle = rib 2 = T4/5 = tracheal bifurcation = start of counting ribs.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Count ribs from the sternal angle (2nd costal cartilage) — the space just below is the 2nd intercostal space.
True ribs 1–7 reach the sternum directly; false 8–10 join the cartilage above; floating 11–12 end free.
The rib head articulates with two vertebrae (demifacets); the tubercle with the transverse process.
Neurovascular bundle lies between the internal and innermost intercostals — VAN in the costal groove.
Intercostal nerves are anterior rami of T1–T11; T12 is the subcostal nerve.
Pump-handle = AP diameter (upper ribs); bucket-handle = transverse diameter (lower ribs).
LIMA is the best coronary bypass conduit; internal thoracic ends as superior epigastric + musculophrenic.
A cervical rib can cause thoracic outlet syndrome.
THORAX__Viscera / Organs:
Why this matters: the thorax holds the two organs that keep you alive minute-to-minute — the lungs and the heart — plus the tubes passing through (trachea, oesophagus). Learn the tracheobronchial tree, the chambers & valves, the coronary supply and the conducting system, and you can read a chest X-ray, an ECG and a murmur from the anatomy up.
Trachea & the Bronchial Tree
Trachea
  • Runs from C6 (cricoid cartilage) to the carina at T4/5 (the sternal angle)
  • Held open by C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings; the posterior gap is bridged by the trachealis muscle (against the oesophagus)
Bronchial tree
  • Main (primary) → lobar (secondary) → segmental (tertiary) bronchi → bronchopulmonary segments
  • The right main bronchus is wider, shorter & more vertical → inhaled objects lodge there
The Lungs
Lobes & fissures
  • Right lung: 3 lobes (upper, middle, lower) — an oblique + a horizontal fissure
  • Left lung: 2 lobes (upper with the lingula, lower) — one oblique fissure; a cardiac notch makes room for the heart
  • The apex rises ~2–3 cm above the medial third of the clavicle
The root (hilum) — “RALS”
  • Contains the main bronchus, pulmonary artery, two pulmonary veins, bronchial vessels, nerves & lymphatics
  • Pulmonary artery: on the Right it is Anterior to the bronchus; on the Left it is Superior (“RALS”)
  • The bronchus is posterior; the pulmonary veins are the most anterior & inferior
Bronchopulmonary segments & a dual blood supply. Each bronchopulmonary segment is a functionally independent unit with its own segmental (tertiary) bronchus & artery — so it can be resected surgically (~10 on the right, 8–10 on the left). The lung has two blood supplies: the pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood for gas exchange, while the bronchial arteries (from the thoracic aorta) supply the lung tissue itself.
The Heart — Chambers
ChamberReceives from / features
Right atriumSVC, IVC & coronary sinus; crista terminalis, pectinate muscles, fossa ovalis (closed foramen ovale)
Right ventricleVia the tricuspid valve; trabeculae carneae, papillary muscles, the moderator band (carries the right bundle branch); pumps to the pulmonary trunk
Left atriumThe four pulmonary veins; smooth-walled & posterior (enlargement can indent the oesophagus)
Left ventricleVia the mitral valve; the thickest wall; forms the apex; pumps to the aorta
Valves & the Conducting System
The four valves
  • Atrioventricular: tricuspid (RA→RV) & mitral/bicuspid (LA→LV) — anchored by chordae tendineae to papillary muscles (prevent prolapse in systole)
  • Semilunar: pulmonary (RV→trunk) & aortic (LV→aorta) — 3 cusps, no chordae; the aortic sinuses give off the coronary arteries
Conducting system
  • SA node (pacemaker) — in the RA wall at the top of the crista terminalis
  • AV node → bundle of His → right & left bundle branches → Purkinje fibres
  • The AV node/bundle is the only electrical route between atria & ventricles (the fibrous skeleton insulates the rest)
Coronary Circulation
Arteries
  • Right coronary artery (RCA) — from the right aortic sinus; gives the SA nodal (~60%), right marginal & (in right-dominance) the posterior interventricular (PDA) branches; supplies the AV node (~90%)
  • Left coronary artery (LCA) → LAD (anterior interventricular) — anterior wall & anterior septum — and the circumflex — lateral wall
  • Dominance = which artery gives the PDA (~70% right-dominant)
Venous drainage
  • Most cardiac veins drain to the coronary sinus (in the posterior AV groove) → the right atrium
  • The anterior cardiac veins & the smallest (Thebesian) veins drain directly to the chambers
The Pericardium
Layers
  • Fibrous pericardium — tough outer sac, fused to the central tendon of the diaphragm & the great vessels (non-distensible)
  • Serous pericardium — a parietal layer (lining the fibrous) and a visceral layer (the epicardium), with the pericardial cavity & its fluid between them
Sinuses, nerve & clinical
  • Transverse sinus (between the arterial & venous outflows — a surgeon’s landmark for cross-clamping) & oblique sinus (behind the left atrium)
  • Sensory supply = the phrenic nerve → referred shoulder pain
  • A rapidly forming effusion → cardiac tamponade (the fibrous sac can’t expand)
Oesophagus & Thymus
Oesophagus
  • A muscular tube from C6 to the cardia at T10/11; upper third skeletal muscle, middle mixed, lower smooth muscle
  • Three constrictions (dysphagia/impaction sites): cricopharyngeus (~15 cm), aortic arch + left bronchus (~25 cm), diaphragmatic hiatus (~40 cm)
  • Lower-third veins drain to the left gastric → portal system → oesophageal varices in portal hypertension
Thymus
  • A bilobed organ in the superior/anterior mediastinum, behind the manubrium
  • Site of T-lymphocyte maturation; large in childhood, then involutes to fat after puberty
  • Associated with myasthenia gravis (thymic hyperplasia / thymoma)
🧠 Mnemonics
Lung root — “RALS”: pulmonary artery is Right Anterior, Left Superior (to the bronchus).
Lobes — Right has 3, Left has 2 (the left lends space to the heart).
Valve flow — Tricuspid → Pulmonary → Mitral → Aortic (the path of blood through the heart).
Moderator band — carries the right bundle branch across the RV to the anterior papillary muscle.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Trachea bifurcates at the carina (T4/5, sternal angle); the right main bronchus is more vertical.
Each bronchopulmonary segment has its own bronchus & artery → surgically resectable.
Lung has a dual supply: pulmonary (gas exchange) + bronchial (tissue nutrition).
Fossa ovalis = closed foramen ovale; moderator band carries the right bundle branch.
AV valves have chordae/papillary muscles; semilunar valves do not; aortic sinuses give the coronaries.
RCA supplies the SA (~60%) & AV (~90%) nodes; LAD the anterior wall/septum.
Coronary sinus drains to the right atrium; the AV node is the only atrio-ventricular electrical link.
Lower oesophageal veins drain to the portal system → varices in portal hypertension.
THORAX__Nerves & Autonomics:
Why this matters: the thorax carries three nerves you must never confuse — the intercostal nerves (somatic, wall), the phrenic (to the diaphragm, anterior to the lung root) and the vagus (parasympathetic, posterior to the root) — plus the sympathetic chain that hands off the splanchnic nerves to the abdomen. Get their courses and the autonomic plexuses, and referred cardiac pain, Horner’s and a hoarse voice all make sense.
Intercostal Nerves
Origin & course
  • The anterior rami of T1–T11 (the T12 ramus = the subcostal nerve)
  • Run in the costal groove, in the plane between the internal & innermost intercostals, below the artery & vein (VAN)
  • T1 gives a large branch to the brachial plexus; T7–T11 continue onto the abdominal wall (thoraco-abdominal nerves)
Branches & supply
  • A collateral branch, a lateral cutaneous branch (splits anterior/posterior) and an anterior cutaneous branch
  • Motor to the intercostal & (lower) abdominal wall muscles
  • Sensory to the overlying skin and the parietal pleura/peritoneum
Dermatome landmarks (learn cold). T2 = axilla · T4 = nipple · T6 = xiphisternum · T10 = umbilicus · T12/L1 = groin. These let you level a sensory loss or a shingles rash.
The Phrenic Nerve (C3–C5)
Course
  • Arises from C3, C4 & C5 (“C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive”); descends on scalenus anterior in the neck
  • In the thorax it runs anterior to the lung root, between the mediastinal pleura & pericardium (with the pericardiacophrenic vessels), to the diaphragm
  • The right phrenic is shorter & straighter; it pierces the diaphragm at the caval opening (T8)
Supply & referred pain
  • Sole motor nerve to the diaphragm; sensory to the central diaphragm, the fibrous/parietal pericardium & the mediastinal pleura
  • Irritation → pain referred to the shoulder tip (C4 dermatome)
The Vagus Nerve (CN X) & Recurrent Laryngeal Nerves
Vagus in the thorax
  • Carries parasympathetic fibres; runs posterior to the lung root (the opposite of the phrenic)
  • Contributes to the cardiac & pulmonary plexuses, then forms the oesophageal plexus
  • Reforms as the anterior (mainly left) & posterior (mainly right) vagal trunks that pass through the oesophageal hiatus (T10)
Recurrent laryngeal nerves
  • Right — loops under the right subclavian artery
  • Left — descends into the thorax to loop under the aortic arch (at the ligamentum arteriosum) before ascending
  • The left’s thoracic course → hoarseness from enlarged mediastinal nodes, an apical lung tumour, or a cardiovascular cause such as an aortic aneurysm / left atrial enlargement (this last being Ortner’s / cardiovocal syndrome)
Phrenic vs vagus at the lung root. The phrenic passes in front of the root (“phrenic = front”); the vagus passes behind it. This single relation is a favourite spotter and explains their different destinations (diaphragm vs the gut/plexuses).
The Sympathetic Chain & Splanchnic Nerves
Sympathetic trunk
  • A chain of paravertebral ganglia running down each side over the rib heads
  • Preganglionic sympathetic neurons arise from the lateral horn of T1–L2; fibres enter via white rami and return via grey rami communicantes
  • Supplies the thoracic viscera (heart, lungs) and, via splanchnics, the abdomen
Thoracic splanchnic nerves
  • Greater (T5–T9) → the coeliac ganglion
  • Lesser (T10–T11) → the aorticorenal / superior mesenteric ganglion
  • Least (T12) → the renal plexus
  • These are preganglionic fibres that pass through the chain without synapsing — to reach the abdominal ganglia
Autonomic Plexuses — Cardiac & Pulmonary
TargetSympatheticParasympathetic (vagus)
Heart (cardiac plexus)↑ rate & force; dilates coronaries↓ rate (& force)
Lungs (pulmonary plexus)Bronchodilation; vasoconstrictionBronchoconstriction; secretomotor

The cardiac plexus (superficial + deep, around the arch & tracheal bifurcation) blends sympathetic fibres (cervical + upper thoracic ganglia) with vagal parasympathetics. The pulmonary plexuses lie anterior & posterior to each lung root.

Referred Cardiac Pain & Horner’s Syndrome
Referred cardiac pain
  • Cardiac pain (visceral afferents) travels back with the sympathetics to T1–T4/5 spinal segments
  • The brain refers it to the matching dermatomes → central chest, left arm, neck & jaw
Horner’s syndrome
  • Interruption of the sympathetic supply to the head (T1 root / stellate ganglion)
  • Ptosis, miosis & anhidrosis (± enophthalmos)
  • A red flag with a Pancoast (apical lung) tumour or lower brachial plexus lesion
🧠 Mnemonics
Phrenic = front of the lung root; vagus passes behind it.
Phrenic roots — “C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive.”
Splanchnics — Greater T5–9 (coeliac), Lesser T10–11, Least T12.
Dermatomes — T4 nipple, T6 xiphoid, T10 umbilicus.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Intercostal nerves = anterior rami T1–T11; T12 = subcostal; T7–T11 also supply the abdominal wall.
Phrenic (C3–5) is the sole motor nerve to the diaphragm and runs anterior to the lung root.
Vagus runs posterior to the root → oesophageal plexus → anterior (L) & posterior (R) vagal trunks.
Left recurrent laryngeal loops under the aortic arch → hoarseness in thoracic disease.
Splanchnic nerves are preganglionic — they pass through the chain without synapsing to reach abdominal ganglia.
Sympathetic → bronchodilation & tachycardia; vagus → bronchoconstriction & bradycardia.
Cardiac pain refers to T1–T4 dermatomes (chest, left arm, jaw).
Horner’s (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) + wasted hand = think Pancoast tumour.
THORAX__Vessels & Lymphatics:
Why this matters: the mediastinum is a plumbing junction — the aorta and its branches leave the heart, the great veins (SVC, IVC, azygos) return blood, and the thoracic duct quietly carries the body’s lymph up to the neck. Learn the aortic branches, the azygos collateral and the thoracic-duct course, and SVC obstruction, chylothorax and aortic disease become anatomy you can localise.
The Aorta
Ascending & arch
  • Ascending aorta — from the LV; its aortic sinuses give the right & left coronary arteries
  • Arch branches (right → left along the arch, proximal to distal): brachiocephalic trunk (→ right common carotid + right subclavian), left common carotid, left subclavian
  • The ligamentum arteriosum (remnant ductus) tethers the arch to the left pulmonary artery — the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks here
Descending thoracic aorta (T4–T12)
  • Visceral branches: bronchial, oesophageal, pericardial & mediastinal
  • Parietal branches: the posterior intercostal arteries (3rd–11th), subcostal & superior phrenic
  • Passes through the aortic hiatus (T12) to become the abdominal aorta
The aortic isthmus. The narrowed segment between the left subclavian artery and the ligamentum arteriosum is the classic site of both coarctation (→ radio-femoral delay, upper-limb hypertension, rib notching) and traumatic aortic rupture (the tethered point in deceleration injury).
The Pulmonary Circulation
Pulmonary arteries
  • The pulmonary trunk leaves the RV and divides into the right & left pulmonary arteries
  • They carry deoxygenated blood to the lungs (the only arteries to do so) for gas exchange
Pulmonary veins
  • Four pulmonary veins (two per lung) return oxygenated blood to the left atrium
  • These are the only veins carrying oxygenated blood
The Great Veins — SVC, Brachiocephalic & IVC
Superior vena cava
  • Formed by the union of the right & left brachiocephalic veins behind the 1st right costal cartilage; ends in the RA (no valves)
  • Each brachiocephalic vein = internal jugular + subclavian (at the venous angle); the left is longer & crosses the midline
  • Just before entering the RA it receives the azygos vein
Inferior vena cava
  • Pierces the diaphragm at the caval opening (T8) (with the right phrenic nerve) and immediately enters the RA
  • Returns all blood from below the diaphragm
The Azygos System
Layout
  • Azygos vein — ascends on the right of the vertebral bodies and arches over the right lung root (T4) to join the SVC
  • Hemiazygos (lower left) & accessory hemiazygos (upper left) cross the midline to drain into the azygos
  • Receives the posterior intercostal, bronchial, oesophageal & pericardial veins
Why it matters
  • It is a key cavo-caval anastomosis — connecting the SVC and IVC systems
  • In SVC or IVC obstruction it enlarges to provide collateral venous return
The Thoracic Duct & Lymphatic Drainage
Thoracic duct
  • The largest lymph vessel; begins at the cisterna chyli (~L1–L2) and enters the thorax through the aortic hiatus (T12)
  • Ascends anterior to the vertebrae (between the aorta & azygos), crossing to the left at ~T4/5
  • Drains into the left venous angle (junction of the left internal jugular & subclavian veins)
  • Drains everything below the diaphragm + the left upper body (i.e. all but the right upper quadrant)
Right lymphatic duct & nodes
  • Right lymphatic duct — drains the right upper quadrant (right head/neck, right arm, right thorax) → the right venous angle
  • Lung lymph flows: bronchopulmonary (hilar) → tracheobronchial (carinal) → paratracheal → bronchomediastinal trunks
Clinical Correlations
SVC obstruction (usually a lung cancer) → facial/arm swelling, distended neck veins, Pemberton’s sign; the azygos provides collateral flow.
Chylothorax — injury to the thoracic duct (surgery/trauma) leaks milky chyle into the pleural space.
Aortic dissection — a tear in the intima; Stanford A (ascending — surgical) vs B (descending — usually medical).
Coarctation at the isthmus → rib notching & radio-femoral delay.
Left recurrent laryngeal palsy from an aortic/arch lesion at the ligamentum arteriosum → hoarseness.
Central venous access targets the internal jugular/subclavian → brachiocephalic → SVC.
🧠 Mnemonics
Arch branches — Brachiocephalic trunk, Left common carotid, Left subclavian (proximal→distal, “ABC” from the right).
Thoracic duct — drains everything except the right upper quadrant (which goes to the right lymphatic duct).
Azygos arches over the right lung root (T4) into the SVC — the SVC↔IVC bypass.
Pulmonary vessels — the only arteries carrying deoxygenated blood & the only veins carrying oxygenated blood.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Aortic arch gives 3 branches: brachiocephalic, left common carotid, left subclavian.
Aortic isthmus (between left subclavian & ligamentum arteriosum) = coarctation & traumatic rupture site.
SVC = union of the two brachiocephalic veins; receives the azygos vein before the RA.
Azygos arches over the right lung root at T4 → SVC; a cavo-caval collateral.
Thoracic duct enters at the aortic hiatus (T12), crosses left at T4/5, drains to the left venous angle.
Thoracic duct drains all of the body except the right upper quadrant.
Chylothorax = thoracic-duct injury; SVC obstruction = commonly lung cancer.
Pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood; pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood.
